errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the mean prerequisite: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier so the child sees the mean chase it while the median holds; the mean is influenced by every value, the median is not
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On tasks (1)-(2) the child reports the mean as the typical value despite the 2 pulling it below the cluster, or claims the median is affected as much as the mean, or deletes the 2 without justification

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares two data sets on the average alone, ignoring the spread — concludes two sets with similar means are 'the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: show two sets with equal means but very different ranges and ask 'are these really the same?'; describing a distribution needs centre AND spread
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child bases the conclusion only on the means and does not mention the range/spread, missing that one class is far more variable

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong average for the data's shape — uses the mean for skewed data (or thinks the mean always sits in the middle of the range) rather than the more representative median/mode
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the choice to the shape: for skewed data or data with an outlier the median represents a typical value better; for most-common/categorical questions the mode; reteach the meaning of the measures via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child defaults to the mean without considering that the skew/outlier makes the median more representative, or expects the mean to be central regardless of shape

errorPatterns.pattern: Range as the extremes, not their difference: gives the range as the two end values rather than the single number highest − lowest
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the range as one number — a distance/spread from lowest to highest — by marking both ends and computing the difference; reteach the term via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child states the range as '2 to 9' (or names lowest and highest) instead of 7

responseLevels.gap: Computes the measures unreliably or gives the range as two numbers; reports the mean regardless of an outlier; compares two sets on the mean alone
responseLevels.full: Computes all four measures, recognises and explains the outlier's differential pull on mean versus median, chooses the appropriate average for the data's shape, and compares two distributions on BOTH centre and spread — transferring the reasoning to a fresh pair of data sets
responseLevels.partial: Correctly computes mean, median, mode and range, but treats the mean as the average to report regardless of skew/outliers, or compares distributions using centre only — has the procedures without the judgement about which measure fits or that spread matters

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small data set with a clear outlier — e.g. hours of sleep: 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 — and a second pair of data sets for comparison (two classes' test scores with similar means but different spreads). Set these tasks and WATCH how they work: (1) 'Find the mean, median, mode and range of the sleep data.' (2) 'Which average best describes a typical night's sleep here? Use it.' (3) 'Compare these two classes and tell me what you can conclude.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint that the 2 is an outlier, nor that comparing needs spread as well as an average.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) forces the choice of average: a child who reports the mean regardless reveals they don't grasp that an outlier makes it unrepresentative, while a child who has the idea switches to the median and says why. Task (3) is built with similar means but different spreads, so a child comparing on the mean alone concludes 'the same' whereas a child who understands distributions cites the spread. The two separate calculation from the judgement the topic is about.

sources.claim: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
sources.source: Batanero, Godino, Vallecillos, Green & Holmes (1994), 'Errors and difficulties in understanding elementary statistical concepts'

sources.claim: A frequent error is to ignore the spread of data; the intuitive notion of variability concerns how much values differ from each other, and different words (variation, dispersion, spread) are open to different interpretations — so describing data needs an explicit measure of spread
sources.source: Batanero et al. (1994), citing Campbell and Loosen et al.

sources.claim: Students' notions of 'average' fragment into most-frequent-value/mode, reasonable value, midpoint and algorithmic relationship — each true in some circumstances but not others — so which average is appropriate depends on the data
sources.source: Batanero et al. (1994), citing Russell & Mokros

sources.claim: KS3 pupils describe, interpret and compare observed distributions of a single variable through appropriate measures of central tendency (mean, mode, median) and spread (range), including consideration of outliers
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3 Statistics)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Describing distributions
topic.description: Describe the distribution of a numerical data set by its centre, spread and overall shape — recognising clusters, gaps, peaks, symmetry or skew (a longer tail on one side) and unusual values — and interpret each feature in the context in which the data were collected, recognising that distributions with similar centres can differ greatly in spread and shape
evidence: Describe a dot plot of 25 pupils' reaction times by its centre (a typical value), its spread (where most values lie and how far they extend) and its shape — naming any cluster, gap, symmetry or skew and unusual value — and link each feature to the context (e.g. a gap between two groups of times might reflect pupils who had practised and pupils who had not)

Compare two distributions with the same mean — e.g. two classes both averaging 60% on a test, one with scores clustered between 52% and 68%, the other spread from 20% to 95% in two separate clusters — and explain what the shared mean hides and why the difference matters in context

Use the context to judge whether an unusual value is more likely a recording error or a genuine extreme (e.g. a reaction time of 4.2 s among times near 0.3 s), and identify claims the display alone cannot support, such as the reason for a skew or that the same pattern would hold for a different group
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a dot plot of how long children in their class took to run 100 m, could they describe where most times bunch up, how spread out they are and whether there are any odd ones out — and suggest a sensible reason for what they see?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Quartiles and interquartile range
topic.description: Find the median, lower quartile and upper quartile of a data set using one explicit convention — order the data, find the median, split the data into a lower and an upper half (leaving out the median itself when there is an odd number of values), and take the median of each half as the lower and upper quartile — while recognising that other textbooks, calculators and software may use slightly different conventions; calculate the interquartile range (IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile) and interpret it as the spread of the middle half of the data; and compare what the range and the IQR reveal, including their different sensitivity to extreme values
evidence: Using the stated convention, find the median (9), lower quartile (6, the median of 3, 5, 6, 7, 8) and upper quartile (14, the median of 11, 12, 14, 15, 21) of the 11 values 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21, giving IQR = 8; and for the 10 values 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, find median 7.5, lower quartile 4 and upper quartile 10, giving IQR = 6

Interpret an IQR in context (e.g. 'the middle half of the puzzle times lie between 6 and 14 minutes, a spread of 8 minutes') and explain that about half of the values lie between the quartiles, with about a quarter below the lower quartile and about a quarter above the upper quartile

Show that changing the largest value from 21 to 40 increases the range from 18 to 37 but leaves the IQR at 8, and use this to decide — and justify — whether the range or the IQR gives the better summary of spread for a data set with an extreme value or a long tail
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} lines up the times their friends took to finish a puzzle, could they find the middle time and the 'quarter-way' times either side of it — and explain why the gap between those quarter-way times is a better guide to how spread out most of the group is than the gap between the very fastest and slowest?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Writing a data summary
topic.description: Write a complete summary of a numerical data set in relation to its context, bringing together: the number of observations; the attribute, how it was measured and its units; a measure of centre with a matching measure of variability, each with units, chosen between median with IQR and mean with MAD; the overall pattern and any striking deviations, interpreted in context; and a justification of that choice by the shape of the distribution and the context (e.g. median and IQR for skewed data or data with extreme values, mean and MAD for roughly symmetric data without extreme values)
evidence: Write a summary of 25 pupils' reaction times that states n, the attribute, how it was measured and the units, a centre and a matching measure of spread with units, and any unusual value
Choose the median and IQR rather than the mean and MAD for a set of journey times with a long tail of slow journeys, and justify the choice by that tail
Rewrite the summary 'the average is 14' as 'the 30 pupils' median journey time is 14 minutes, with the middle half of times between 9 and 22 minutes'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} timed how long 25 friends took to solve a puzzle, could they write a short report saying how many were timed, how the times were measured, a typical time and how spread out the times were (with units) — and mention any time that stood out?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing data sets digitally
topic.description: Interpret and compare data sets for nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays (side-by-side column graphs with ordinal categories in a common order, back-to-back dot plots) made with digital tools, processing the data (percentages, ranges) and comparing distributions by mode, range and shape
evidence: Make a side-by-side column graph in a spreadsheet comparing the favourite sports (nominal) of Year 3 and Year 6 students and state the mode for each group

Compare two classes' ratings of 'How much do you enjoy reading?' (never, sometimes, often, always) as percentages on side-by-side graphs with the categories in the same order, and say which class's ratings sit higher on the scale
Compare two classes' jump distances by mode, range and shape using back-to-back dot plots made with a digital tool
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has survey results from two classes of different sizes, can they use a spreadsheet to make a side-by-side graph, turn the counts into percentages, and compare the two fairly?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Critiquing statistics in the media
topic.description: Identify statistically informed arguments in traditional and digital media and critique their methods, data representations (e.g. truncated axes, distorted pictographs, selective data) and conclusions
evidence: Explain how a bar graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 exaggerates a small difference
Identify the sample size and who was surveyed in a news claim such as '9 out of 10 kids prefer Brand X' and judge whether the conclusion is justified
Rewrite a misleading online headline so that it matches what the data actually show
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an ad saying '9 out of 10 kids prefer this cereal' or a graph with a stretched-out axis, can they ask who was asked and whether the graph makes the difference look bigger than it is?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Populations, samples and fair sampling
topic.description: Distinguish a population from a sample drawn from it; explain why a convenient or biased sample (choosing whoever is easiest to reach, volunteers, or a group linked to the answer) can misrepresent the population; explain that random selection gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, which tends to produce representative samples — while recognising that any single random sample can still, by chance, be unrepresentative
evidence: In a described survey (e.g. a school asks 40 of its 800 pupils about the lunch menu), identify the population and the sample, and explain why a sample is used instead of asking everyone

Identify the selection bias in a sampling method (e.g. asking people leaving a gym how often they exercise, or surveying only the lunch queue on pizza day), explain the direction in which it would likely distort the result, and propose a better method using random selection from the whole population (e.g. drawing names from the full school register)

Explain the difference between random selection and simply choosing whoever is easiest to reach, and explain — with an example such as a random sample of 10 pupils that happens to contain mostly Year 7s — why random sampling makes a representative sample likely but does not guarantee it
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a school wanted to know what all its pupils think of the lunch menu but only asked children in the lunch queue on pizza day, could {{name}} explain why that might give a misleading answer — and suggest a fairer way to choose who to ask, like picking names at random from the whole school list?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing two populations
topic.description: Use measures of centre and variability calculated from random samples of two populations to make informal comparative inferences about those populations (e.g. whether words in a Grade 7 science book are generally longer than words in a Grade 4 science book): check that each sample was randomly drawn from the population it is meant to describe and is reasonably representative; weigh the difference between the sample centres against the variability within the samples and against how much centres vary from one random sample to another; and state qualified conclusions ('generally', 'on average', 'probably') rather than claiming every member of one population exceeds every member of the other — recognising that a small difference between two samples may be due to chance alone
evidence: Compare random samples of 20 word lengths from two books (means 6.2 and 4.4 letters, both MADs about 0.9) and conclude that the first book probably uses longer words on average
Explain why surveying volunteers at one school's sports club cannot support a conclusion that all pupils at that school are fitter than pupils at another school
Judge that a 1-point difference between two sample medians is not convincing when repeated random samples from one population give medians that vary by about 3 points
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} randomly picked 20 words from a Year 7 science book and 20 from a Year 4 science book, could they use the averages and spreads to decide whether the older book generally uses longer words — and explain why they'd say 'probably' rather than 'definitely'?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Estimating from a sample
topic.description: Use data from a random sample to estimate a characteristic of the population, such as a proportion, total count, or mean; present the result as an estimate rather than an exact population measurement; state the assumptions the inference relies on (the sample was randomly drawn from the population being described and is reasonably representative) and explain how the conclusion is limited or invalid when those assumptions fail
evidence: Use a sample proportion to estimate a population count — e.g. 18 of a random sample of 60 pupils walk to school, so estimate about 270 of the school's 900 pupils walk — and state the answer as an approximate estimate rather than an exact count

Use the mean of a random sample (e.g. the mean weekly reading time of 25 randomly chosen pupils) to estimate the population mean, and explain why the true population mean is likely to be close to, but probably not exactly equal to, the sample mean

State the assumptions behind an estimate and explain why it becomes unreliable or invalid when they fail — e.g. using a sample of only Year 7 pupils to estimate for the whole school, or using a volunteer online poll — and identify what can and cannot be concluded from the data
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that 12 out of 40 randomly chosen pupils at their school play an instrument, could they estimate how many of the school's 600 pupils play one — and explain why that number is a sensible estimate rather than an exact count?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: How far apart two groups are
topic.description: Compare two numerical distributions with similar variability shown on a shared scale (e.g. dot plots) in two distinct ways: (1) judge their actual visual overlap directly from the displays — how much of each group's data lies among the other group's values; and (2) separately, find the difference between their centres and express it as a multiple of a clearly named measure of variability of either group, using matching measures (difference in means ÷ MAD, or difference in medians ÷ IQR), interpreting a larger multiple as centres that are further apart relative to the typical spread. Recognise that the same difference in centres means more when the variability is small, and that for similarly shaped, roughly symmetric, single-peaked distributions a larger multiple usually goes with less overlap — but that the ratio alone does not determine overlap: skew, clusters, gaps or outliers can make the visible overlap greater or smaller than the ratio suggests, so overlap is always checked on the display; and this simple ratio is only appropriate when the two variabilities are similar
evidence: Describe two dot plots of team heights drawn on the same scale as overlapping a lot, a little, or hardly at all, pointing to the range of heights the two teams share
Express a 10 cm difference in mean heights as about 2 MADs when each team's MAD is about 5 cm, naming MAD as the measure used
Use two dot plots whose means are 2 MADs apart, one with a long tail towards the other group, to explain why they overlap more than the 2-MAD gap alone would suggest
topic.assessmentPrompt: If the basketball team's average height is 10 cm more than the football team's, and players on each team are typically about 5 cm from their own team's average, could {{name}} explain that the gap is about twice the usual spread — and then look at a chart of both teams' heights to check how much they actually overlap, rather than guessing it from that number?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: How samples vary
topic.description: Generate or compare several random samples of the same size from the same population (by drawing physically — returning and remixing the items before each new sample — from a list, or by simulation), observe that their estimates differ by chance, and use the spread of those estimates to judge how uncertain a single estimate or prediction is — distinguishing chance variation between random samples from the consistent error caused by a biased sampling method, and distinguishing variation between sample estimates from the variation among individual observations within a sample
evidence: Take or are given several random samples of the same size from one population (e.g. draw 20 counters from a bag without looking, record them, return all 20 and mix thoroughly, then draw the next 20 — five times; or five random samples of 20 names from a list), calculate each sample's proportion or mean, and show that the estimates differ

Explain that equal-sized random samples give different estimates because of chance in which individuals are selected, so a different result does not mean a sample was wrong — and contrast this with a biased method whose estimates are consistently too high or too low

Use the spread of several sample estimates (e.g. 'the estimates ranged from 25% to 40%') to say how far off a single estimate might be, and explain why one sample cannot make a prediction certain and why larger samples tend to give estimates that vary less

Distinguish the variation among individual observations within one sample (e.g. pupils' sleep times in one sample range from 6 to 11 hours) from the variation between sample estimates (e.g. the means of five samples of 20 pupils range from 8.6 to 9.3 hours), and explain why sample means usually vary much less than the individual values they are calculated from
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class takes turns drawing 20 sweets from the same big jar without looking — counting the red ones, then putting all 20 back and giving the jar a good shake before the next person draws — could {{name}} explain why each person gets a slightly different number of reds, and use the spread of everyone's results to say how sure they can be about the fraction of red sweets in the whole jar?
